entries.name: Orthodox Christmas (Julian calendar)
entries.capsule: Christmas for Russian Orthodox parishes that keep the Julian calendar, falling on January 7.
entries.dateRule: December 25 on the Julian calendar, which is January 7 on the Gregorian calendar from 1900 to 2099. The 2026 holiday season's Christmas falls on January 7, 2027.
entries.whatItMarks: The birth of Jesus, for churches that follow the Julian calendar.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Russian Orthodox parishes in Minneapolis and Fridley (St. Panteleimon; Resurrection of Christ Church and Skete) post service schedules in Russian and English, but no 2027 Christmas schedule was posted when checked. Many Russian-speaking households are Jewish, Protestant or not religious and do not keep this date.

sources.title: Resurrection of Christ Church and Skete

entries.name: Orthodox Easter (Pascha)
entries.capsule: The most important Orthodox Christian feast, usually later than Western Easter; April 12 in 2026, May 2 in 2027.
entries.dateRule: First Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, reckoned on the Julian calendar.
entries.whatItMarks: The resurrection of Jesus in Eastern Christian tradition.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Kept by Russian Orthodox parishes such as St. Panteleimon in Minneapolis and Resurrection of Christ in Fridley, and by Orthodox Church in America parishes. No dated Minnesota Pascha event for Russian speakers was found.

entries.whatItMarks: The 1945 end of the Second World War in Europe, as remembered in the Soviet Union and its successor states.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: No public Minnesota Victory Day event was found for 2025 or 2026. War memory appears in community life in other ways: a 2010 documentary by Minnesota's VOICE program on Soviet Jewish soldiers, and readers' World War II memories in Zerkalo magazine (2016).

entries.name: New Year (Novy God)
entries.capsule: The big secular winter holiday of Soviet times, with a decorated tree and Grandfather Frost; still central for some families.
entries.dateRule: January 1, with the main celebration on the night of December 31.

entries.whatItMarks: The new year; in Soviet times it replaced Christmas as the main family winter holiday.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Mostly at home. Staff at Smak, an Anoka grocery, told Macalester students that although New Year's is traditionally the biggest holiday, families here often adopt Christmas-season habits; the store is busiest at Thanksgiving and Christmas. No public 2025 or 2026 Minnesota New Year (yolka) event was found.

entries.name: Maslenitsa (Butter Week)
entries.capsule: A pancake-filled farewell to winter in the week before Orthodox Lent; TMORA held a blini and folk-song evening in 2026.
entries.dateRule: The week before Orthodox Great Lent, ending the Sunday 49 days before Pascha. Dates shown are the week of Maslenitsa; organizers choose their own event days.
entries.whatItMarks: The end of winter and the last week before the Lenten fast, with blini (pancakes), songs and games.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: The Museum of Russian Art held 'Maslenitsa: Russian Pancakes & Songs' with its folk group Nitka at its Education Center on Feb. 17, 2026 ($35 members, $40 others). St. Panteleimon Russian Orthodox Church also holds Maslenitsa events, according to Macalester's guide.

entries.name: St. Panteleimon Patronal Feast (Minneapolis)
alsoKnownAs: Feast of St. Panteleimon the Healer
entries.capsule: Minneapolis's Russian Orthodox parish honors its patron saint each August with vigil, liturgy, procession and a banquet.
entries.dateRule: Feast of St. Panteleimon, July 27 on the Julian calendar (August 9 Gregorian), with the vigil the evening before. The parish sets its own celebration days.
entries.whatItMarks: The parish's patron saint, a healer; in 2026 also the parish's 70th anniversary (1956-2026).
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: In 2026 Bishop Spyridon of Chicago and Mid-America led an all-night vigil on Aug. 8 and a Divine Liturgy, cross procession and banquet on Aug. 9, with clergy from Fridley, Fargo, Ann Arbor and Des Plaines.

entries.name: Anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
entries.capsule: A painful date for many Russian-speaking households; marked in Minnesota with vigils and anti-war gatherings.
entries.whatItMarks: The start of the full-scale war in 2022, which divided some families and friendships and brought new arrivals from both Ukraine and Russia.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: On the first anniversary in 2023, the Lowry Avenue Bridge in Minneapolis was lit blue and gold and a candlelight vigil was held there; Zerkalo's publisher planned to attend. Russian anti-war protests were held at the State Capitol in 2023. This is a remembrance, not a celebration; the Ukrainian community page covers its own observances.
